questions.q: Per this lesson, why is '188 rows don't match the expected email pattern' described as 'a fact' rather than automatically 'a problem'?
options: Because whether it's a real problem requires interpretation — checking scale, context, and whether it's new before concluding it's actionable
Because 188 is always too small a number to matter in any table
Because pattern profiling queries are never reliable
Because only NULL counts can ever indicate real problems
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that a raw profiling number is a fact, not a conclusion — interpreting it correctly requires asking further questions before acting.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say '188 mismatched rows out of 10,000' and '188 mismatched rows out of 200' should be treated very differently?
options: Because the same raw count represents a vastly different percentage (scale) depending on the total row count
Because 188 out of 200 is always a data entry error
Because larger tables always have better data quality
Because SQL Server treats the two cases identically regardless of scale
questions.explain: The 'what's the scale' question is explicit that the same raw count can mean 'edge case' (1.9%) or 'fundamentally broken' (94%) depending on the denominator.

questions.q: In the worked example, what should you do before reporting '188 bad emails' as a confirmed data quality problem?
options: Pull a sample of the actual values to check whether they're genuinely malformed or just legitimate-but-unusual formats the pattern check wasn't built to handle
Immediately delete all 188 rows from the table
Assume all 188 are errors without further review
Rewrite the entire Customer table from scratch
questions.explain: The lesson warns that skipping this sampling step can lead to 'fixing' perfectly good data, or training a future rule on a flawed assumption about what 'valid' looks like.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what makes a profiling finding 'actionable'?
options: A specific person can make a specific decision based on it
It contains at least 1,000 rows
It was generated using a JOIN rather than a simple SELECT
It was found using the GROUP BY clause specifically
questions.explain: The lesson states that if a finding doesn't change any decision anyone would make, it isn't worth escalating yet — actionability is tied to a specific person and a specific decision.

questions.q: Which question in this lesson's four-question framework can only be answered by measuring the same thing over time, not from a single profiling pass?
options: Is this new, or has it always been this way?
What's the scale?
Who actually needs to know?
Is this actually abnormal, or did I just notice it?
questions.explain: Telling whether a finding represents a recent change versus a long-standing steady state requires a baseline from repeated monitoring (Lesson 26), not a one-time profiling query.
